context: The three poets walk in single file along the outer rim of the terrace, with the fire on one side and the drop on the other. Virgil keeps warning Dante to mind his footing.

note: Late afternoon. The sun is low in the west, and the blue of the sky there is paling toward evening.

quote: made the flames appear more red
note: Fire looks pale in sunlight and redder in shade. Where Dante's shadow falls on the flames they darken, and the souls see that he has a real body.

context: In Canto 25 Statius explained that the dead shape a body out of air. It can be seen and can suffer, but it casts no shadow, so Dante's shadow gives him away.

note: The seventh and highest terrace, where lust is purged. The fire of desire is burned away by real fire. The souls want the cleansing, so they take care never to step out of the flames.
Virgil and Statius walk ahead. Statius, a Roman poet, joined them in Canto 21 and is climbing to Heaven.
People of the hottest lands Dante's world knew of.
A second band of the lustful, walking round the terrace the opposite way. The speaker will explain at lines 77–82 who they are.
A chaste greeting, like the "holy kiss" Saint Paul asks Christians to give one another (Romans 16:16). The souls who once lingered over kisses now exchange one and hurry on.
The cities God destroyed with fire from heaven in Genesis 19. Medieval readers took their sin to be sex between men. Each terrace has examples of its sin that the souls call out to shame themselves.

context: The example of lust shouted by the first group, whose desire was for the opposite sex but ran beyond all restraint.

note: Dante names the Riphaean mountains, a range the ancients placed in the far north. The simile is imaginary: real cranes all migrate the same way. "Warm sands" are the deserts of Africa.
In Canto 25 the souls were singing a hymn that asks God to burn lust out of the heart, and calling out examples of chastity between verses.
He did not die young or old. He has not died at all, and his body is here with him.

context: Usually taken to be Beatrice, who sent Virgil to Dante. Some readers think of the Virgin Mary, who first moved Beatrice to act (Inferno 2).

quote: full of love and spreads most wide
context: It "spreads most wide" because it lies outside all the other heavens and holds them within it.

note: Dante tells the souls he is a writer and will set down what they say. The poem is that record.

context: Roman gossip said the young Caesar had been the lover of Nicomedes, king of Bithynia. The historian Suetonius reports that his soldiers sang jokes about it at his triumph and that his enemies called him "queen".

note: Dante's word, from the myth of Hermaphroditus, who was joined with a nymph into one body, male and female. It means only that their lust was between man and woman.
The rule of reason, which should govern desire. Their sin was not loving the opposite sex but loving without measure, as animals follow appetite.
Pasiphaë again. The "bestial wood" is the wooden cow she climbed into.

context: Dante meets the poet he calls his father in the art of love poetry. Poets of love fill this terrace: love was their subject, and its excess their sin.

quote: because I repented before my final hour
note: Guido died about 1276, less than 25 years before. He is already this high on the mountain because he repented in good time. Those who put it off until death must first wait outside the gate, on the slopes below.

From the Thebaid of Statius, who is walking just ahead. Hypsipyle was nursing King Lycurgus's baby son when a snake killed him. The king condemned her to death, and her two grown sons, long parted from her, broke through the crowd to embrace her.
The sons ran to their mother. Dante feels the same joy but does not run to Guido: the fire holds him back.

Father in poetry. Guinizzelli began the kind of love poem that Dante and his friends developed, which Dante named the "sweet new style" in Canto 24. "My betters" is Dante's modesty about his fellow poets.

context: Guido means that even the river of forgetting will not wipe out his memory of Dante's words. Dante will reach its bank in Canto 28.

note: Dante's Italian says "the modern usage": writing poetry in the spoken language rather than in Latin. In Dante's day it was still a young practice.

quote: a better craftsman of our mother tongue
note: Guido turns the praise aside, as the souls of Purgatory do. The Italian is "miglior fabbro del parlar materno", literally a better smith. T. S. Eliot borrowed "il miglior fabbro" to dedicate The Waste Land to Ezra Pound.
No romances by Arnaut are known. The Italian is usually read to mean that he outdid everyone who wrote love poems or prose romances, that is, every writer in the vernacular languages of France.

context: Dante's Italian says "the one from the Limousin", the region around Limoges. Dante himself had praised Giraut highly in an earlier work. Here he ranks Arnaut above him.
"Ancients" means the older generation, who went on praising Guittone out of habit. Dante's circle defined its new style against him.

quote: where Christ is abbot of the college
note: Heaven, pictured as a monastery with Christ at its head and the blessed as its community.

The Lord's Prayer. The dead in Purgatory are helped by the prayers of the living. Guido asks for all of it except what he no longer needs: the last request, to be kept from temptation, since these souls cannot sin. The proud made the same point in Canto 11.

quote: Your courteous request so pleases me
note: In the original, Arnaut's eight lines are not in Italian but in Provençal, the language of the troubadours: "Tan m'abellis vostre cortes deman". It is the longest passage in a foreign tongue in the whole poem, and Dante's tribute to him.

context: Arnaut's poems were famous for being difficult. Dante gives him a speech of great plainness: he weeps for his past and sings for what is coming.

note: His life of love and the poetry that celebrated it. Like Guido, he names his sin without excuse and looks ahead with joy.
The Italian word means to refine, as a goldsmith refines metal in fire. T. S. Eliot quotes this line in Italian near the end of The Waste Land.
